excerpt: Why insurers ignore or delay a demand letter after a personal injury claim, what the silence usually means, and the steps that get a response in Georgia and South Carolina.
keyTakeaways: Your deadline to sue does not pause while an insurer ignores your demand: two years from the injury in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). In a Georgia motor-vehicle case, a demand prepared with a lawyer is a pre-suit offer under O.C.G.A. § 9-11-67.1 and must give the insurer at least 30 days to accept and at least 40 days to pay. Neither state sets a statutory deadline for the other driver's insurer to answer a demand. The bad-faith penalties in O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6 and S.C. Code § 38-59-40 apply only to your own insurer; against the other driver's insurer, the remedy is a lawsuit against the driver, not a bad-faith claim. Unfair claim practices, such as failing to acknowledge claim communications with reasonable promptness, can be reported to the state insurance regulator.

faqs.question: What is a demand letter?
faqs.answer: A written demand for a stated amount, sent to open settlement negotiations, that sets out fault, the injuries and losses, and the records supporting them. In a Georgia motor-vehicle case, a pre-suit offer prepared with a lawyer must contain the material terms in O.C.G.A. § 9-11-67.1, including an acceptance date at least 30 days out and a payment date at least 40 days out, and enclose the records the insurer needs to evaluate the claim.

faqs.question: Why is the insurance company ignoring my demand letter?
faqs.answer: Insurers know that financial pressure builds while medical bills accumulate and income is lost, and a claimant under that pressure is more likely to accept less than the claim is worth. Silence can also mean the insurer is waiting on records it needs to evaluate the claim. Both states treat failing to acknowledge claim communications with reasonable promptness, and failing to attempt a fair settlement once liability is reasonably clear, as unfair claim practices (O.C.G.A. § 33-6-34; S.C. Code § 38-59-20).

faqs.question: What is the normal timeline after a demand letter is sent?
faqs.answer: Neither Georgia nor South Carolina sets a statutory deadline for the other driver's insurer to answer a demand. In Georgia, a § 9-11-67.1 demand must give the insurer at least 30 days to accept and at least 40 days to pay, so no response to it is overdue before day 30. What does not move is your deadline to sue: two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33), three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Silence that runs toward that deadline is a signal the claim needs escalating rather than more waiting.

faqs.question: What should I do if the insurer will not respond?
faqs.answer: Escalate rather than repeat. An attorney who knows how insurers and adjusters operate can apply formal pressure and, where necessary, file suit, which changes the calculation for the insurer entirely. The two formal escalations are a complaint to the state insurance regulator and a lawsuit against the at-fault driver filed before the deadline to sue.

faqs.question: Can I write a demand letter myself?
faqs.answer: You can, and many people do. The risk is undervaluing the claim or omitting losses that are hard to recover later, which is why having the letter prepared or reviewed by a lawyer is usually worthwhile. Two cautions: in Georgia only a demand prepared with a lawyer is a § 9-11-67.1 offer, and both states cut recovery by your share of fault. Georgia bars recovery at 50% or more (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33); South Carolina bars it when your fault is greater than the other driver's (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.).
